cases.title: Every inline mark reachable before this suite, in CT_RPr order
cases.notes: The floor. These seven were the ENTIRE reachable run vocabulary before this suite; if any moves, every later row is measuring against a shifted baseline. Also pins that an unstyled run emits no w:rPr at all rather than an empty one.

cases.title: size is points; w:sz is HALF-points, and w:szCs moves with it
cases.notes: 7.5pt -> 15 is the row that matters: half-points are the unit, so a half-point size is exactly representable and must not round to 14 or 16. szCs is not decoration - omit it and a complex-script run silently keeps the default size.

cases.title: font sets ascii, hAnsi and cs together
cases.notes: Three attributes, not one. Setting only w:ascii leaves Word free to pick a different face for anything it classes as high-ANSI or complex-script, which is how one run renders in two fonts.

cases.title: smallCaps
letterSpacing is points; w:spacing is TWENTIETHS of a point, and may be negative
cases.notes: Zero is ABSENT, not w:val=0 - tracking of zero is already the default, and emitting it would make every untracked run differ from the same run written before this feature existed. Negative tracking is legal and is how a large display size gets tightened.

cases.title: The full CT_RPr sequence, and where each new property inserts
cases.notes: CT_RPr is an xsd:sequence, so this order is the schema's and not a preference: rStyle, rFonts, b, i, smallCaps, strike, color, spacing, sz, szCs, u, shd. The second run pins that `code` keeps Consolas even when the run also asks for a font - code is the more specific request.

cases.title: align, including the two values that are not identity mappings
cases.notes: justify is w:val=both in WordprocessingML, and left is the default so it emits nothing - an explicit left and an absent align must produce the same paragraph, or a round-trip invents a property that was never asked for.

cases.title: spaceBefore / spaceAfter are points; w:spacing is twentieths
cases.notes: spaceAfter: 0 must EMIT w:after=0. Unlike letterSpacing, zero here is not the default - the document defaults put 160 twips after every paragraph, so an omitted zero leaves 8pt of air under a line that asked for none. The single most load-bearing row for dense layout.

cases.title: lineHeight is a multiple; w:line is 240ths with lineRule auto
cases.notes: One w:spacing element carries before, after, line and lineRule together - emitting two would be invalid. w:lineRule=auto is what makes w:line a multiple of single spacing rather than an exact height.

cases.title: indentLeft / indentRight in points
keepNext
cases.notes: keepNext: false emits nothing rather than w:keepNext w:val=0. Both are legal OOXML and they differ only when a style already set it; the model has no style inheritance to override, so the simpler emission is the honest one.

cases.title: shading fills the paragraph band
cases.notes: Lower-case hex in, upper-case hex out. Word accepts either; the engines must agree on one or two of them emit different bytes for the same document.

cases.title: borders, including an explicit none
cases.notes: 0.75pt -> w:sz 6, because border width is in EIGHTHS of a point while every other length here is twentieths. style: none becomes w:val=nil with no width and no colour - a nil border is the only way to remove one, and a zero width is not it.

cases.title: The full CT_PPr sequence
cases.notes: CT_PPr order: pStyle, keepNext, numPr, pBdr, shd, spacing, ind, jc, outlineLvl. w:jc coming AFTER w:ind and w:spacing is the one most likely to be got wrong by emitting properties in the order the model happens to list them.

cases.title: A heading is a paragraph and takes the same properties, after its pStyle
cases.notes: Headings could not be aligned or spaced at all before this suite, so every section label in a real layout had to be a bold paragraph impersonating a heading - and therefore appeared in no navigation pane and no table of contents.

cases.title: A table with no options - the reconciled default all three engines now emit
cases.notes: THE RECONCILIATION ROW. Node referenced a shared w:tblStyle LastWordTable plus a w:tblLook, taking borders and cell margins from styles.xml; PHP and Python inlined w:tblBorders and set no cell margins at all. A named style cannot vary per table instance, so per-table borders forced everything inline - and the style's more generous 60/108 cell margins became the shared default rather than being dropped on the floor.

cases.title: widths are relative weights over the section's content width
cases.notes: Weights, not percentages and not points: [30,40,30] and [3,4,3] are the same table. w:tblLayout fixed appears only when widths are given - without it Word re-fits columns to their content and the requested proportions are advisory. The grid must sum to the content width EXACTLY, so any rounding remainder goes to the last column.

cases.title: The grid sums to the content width exactly, remainder on the last column
cases.notes: 9360 divides by three exactly, so this row proves the equal case; 0017 and the reference document cover uneven ones. The rule is pinned because three engines rounding independently is how one language ends up with a table a twip narrower than the other two.

cases.title: width is a percentage of the content width; w:tblW pct is FIFTIETHS of a percent
cases.notes: The grid narrows with the table. Emitting w:tblW pct while leaving the grid at full width hands Word two contradictory answers, and which one wins differs between Word and every other renderer.

cases.title: align on a table is w:jc in tblPr, between tblW and tblBorders
cases.notes: Only meaningful on a table narrower than the text column, which is why this row sets width too.

cases.title: Per-table borders, including inside edges and explicit none
cases.notes: A rule across the top and hairline dividers between columns, with nothing else - the KPI band construct. CT_TblBorders order is top, left, bottom, right, insideH, insideV.

cases.title: cellPadding sets w:tblCellMar for every cell at once
A cell with no options emits its width and nothing else
A header row shades its cells - one grey, in all three engines
cases.notes: E7E7E7 was PHP's and Python's; Node shaded the same row F2F2F2 and took its header bold from a table style instead of a w:b run, so one input produced two different greys AND two different models on read-back. Node moved to the majority. Changing this row again is a decision about all three engines at once.

cases.title: Per-cell shading
cases.notes: One tinted cell inside an otherwise plain grid was the construct that could not be built at all: shading existed only as the hardcoded header grey keyed off row.header, so tinting a single cell meant tinting its whole row.

cases.title: Per-cell borders
cases.notes: A 2pt accent rule over one card and nothing over its neighbours. CT_TcBorders order is top, left, bottom, right.

cases.title: Per-cell padding overrides the table's
cases.notes: 5.4pt -> 108 twips is the value Word itself uses for default side margins, and is why the shared default reads as an odd number rather than a round one.

cases.title: valign
cases.notes: top is emitted explicitly even though it is Word's default, because unlike align:left it costs nothing to state and a cell that says top is a cell whose author decided.

cases.title: colSpan is w:gridSpan, and the cell takes the width of every column it covers
cases.notes: The grid is three columns because a row's WIDTH is the sum of its cells' spans, not its cell count. Getting that wrong gives a table whose first row is short by a column and whose borders do not line up with the rows below it.

cases.title: rowSpan is w:vMerge restart plus a synthesised continuation in each following row
cases.notes: The author writes ONE cell and the next row lists only its own remaining cell, HTML-style. The writer synthesises the continuation, because a row missing a cell is a malformed table and Word repairs it by shifting everything left. The continuation carries the origin's shading and nothing else: without the fill the merged block renders striped, and with the origin's borders it would draw a rule straight through its own middle.

cases.title: The full CT_TcPr sequence
cases.notes: CT_TcPr order: tcW, gridSpan, vMerge, tcBorders, shd, tcMar, vAlign. Also pins that a cell can span both directions at once and that the continuation inherits the gridSpan - a continuation of a different width is the other way to make Word repair the table.

cases.title: The default page, unchanged
cases.notes: US Letter with one-inch margins. Pinned so that the next row is visibly a change rather than a guess.

cases.title: page.margins in points
cases.notes: A one-page business document does not fit inside one-inch margins, which is why the page block exists at all rather than being deferred as cosmetic.

cases.title: page.size and orientation; landscape swaps the axes AND sets w:orient
cases.notes: Swapping w and h without w:orient gives a page that is the right shape and prints portrait. Both are required.

cases.title: Narrower margins make a WIDER table - the grid comes from the section, not a constant
cases.notes: 12240 - 720 - 720 = 10800 twips of content, against 9360 at the default margins. All three engines carried 9360 as a literal, so before this row a document that narrowed its margins got a table that no longer matched its own page - too narrow, and silently so.

cases.title: Every run property survives a write and a read
cases.notes: Colours come back upper-case because that is what was written; the model is case-insensitive on the way in and canonical on the way out.

cases.title: Every paragraph property survives
cases.notes: A border with no explicit style reads back with no explicit style. The reader omits style when it is single, colour when it is auto and space when it is zero, because otherwise reading a document written from a model would return a bigger model than went in - and a second write would then differ from the first.

cases.title: A default table surfaces NO options - defaults are not invented on read
cases.notes: The writer emits borders, cell margins and a w:tcW for every cell whether or not the model asked. If the reader reported those back, every document written before this feature existed would come back carrying options nobody set - and the equal-column grid would come back as explicit widths. The rule is: a value the writer would have produced anyway is not surfaced, and the equal-split grid is compared against the split the writer computes rather than tested for exact equality, so a three-column table whose width does not divide by three is still recognised as equal.

cases.title: Table and cell properties survive
cases.notes: Widths come back as the weights that produced them: 25/25/50 of 9360 is 2340/2340/4680, which divides back exactly. Partial padding stays partial - a cell that set only top and bottom does not acquire left and right.

cases.title: Both merges survive, and the synthesised continuation cells disappear again
cases.notes: The hard direction. The file contains three cells in the second row - the vMerge continuation the writer synthesised, plus the authored spanning cell - and the reader has to drop the continuation and put the rowSpan back on the cell two rows up. A reader that returns the continuation gives a model that writes to a DIFFERENT file than the one it just read.

cases.title: page and the document defaults survive
cases.notes: Defaults are omitted on read here too: a Letter portrait page with one-inch margins surfaces no `page` key at all, and Calibri at 11pt surfaces no defaults - see 0032, which is the same document with none of them set.

cases.title: A header row does NOT round-trip, and this is the shape of the loss
cases.notes: KNOWN AND DELIBERATE. `header: true` makes the writer bold the row's runs, and the reader honestly reports the bold it finds - so the model that comes out is not the model that went in. The alternative was to stop bolding header rows, which changes every existing consumer's output, or to have the reader strip bold from header rows, which would discard bold an author really did ask for. The asymmetry is pinned here so it is a documented property rather than a surprise; the shading is NOT surfaced, because that one the reader can attribute to `header` unambiguously.

cases.title: The reference document: a business one-pager, read back to exactly the model that wrote it

runs.text: Sample Client Ltd (SCL)  |  Business Case  |  15 January 2026
The problem is not record matching.
SCL's overpayments passed the standard three-way match. The gap sits upstream: validating whether the
source document itself complies with the agreement
agreement → quote → authorisation → source document → invoice
Reads agreements, amendments and statements of work, then validates every source document against contractual rates, charge types and conditions before approval.
Traverses agreement, quote, authorisation, source document and invoice to determine whether a charge was commercially authorised, not merely matched.
Detects one-time approvals that quietly recur across sites and months, surfacing the exception creep that transaction-by-transaction systems miss.
Overpayments already identified, not modelled exposure.
Simple annualisation of the confirmed audit finding.
Only ~5% is currently spot-checked; ~40% of service contracts carry variable surcharges.
Ten months billed at $4.20 / unit while the index price fell to $3.40.
Complement the ERP, don't replace it.

The ERP can continue handling supplier transactions and invoice-to-document matching. Example Analytics becomes the upstream intelligence layer that determines whether the source document should have been approved in the first place.
Run a tailored validation against SCL's own audit fact patterns: standby-rate compliance, recurring one-off charges, and surcharge validation. Confirm total surcharge spend to complete the ROI model.
Prepared for the Finance and Accounts Payable leads  |  Prepared by Example Analytics

cases.notes: THE ACCEPTANCE ARTIFACT, reduced to the one claim a fixture can make about it. It exercises a KPI stat band, a dark full-bleed callout, a bordered three-column grid with one tinted cell and both merge directions, a three-card row with white gutters cut by a 3pt inside border, a definition table with a tinted label column, a two-tint closing pair and a footer rule - roughly forty distinct property emissions in one document. Whether it LOOKS right is not a fixture's business and is checked by rendering it; what this row proves is that nothing the writer emitted is invisible to the reader. Its content is invented and neutral: it reproduces the structure of a real client one-pager and none of its text, names, figures or branding.

cases.title: The fixpoint check is capable of returning false
cases.notes: The control for 0043. Without it, an implementation of roundTripFixpoint that returns a hardcoded true passes the acceptance row and the suite reports success over nothing. 0042 is the same document, spelled out.
